title: Split or Torn Cat Claw: Safe First Steps When the Quick Is Exposed
description: Learn what to do when a cat splits or tears a claw, how to control minor bleeding, and when exposed quick, pain, swelling, or infection needs veterinary care.
summary: A split or torn claw can be very painful because the quick contains nerves and blood vessels. A claw may snag on carpet, furniture, wire, or a scratching surface, or it may tear during a jump or struggle.
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Cat with a split front claw being gently examined without graphic injury
content:
A split or torn claw can be very painful because the quick contains nerves and blood vessels. A claw may snag on carpet, furniture, wire, or a scratching surface, or it may tear during a jump or struggle. Some injuries affect only the hard outer shell, while deeper tears expose living tissue.

What This Change Can Mean

If bleeding is mild, keep your cat calm and apply gentle pressure with clean gauze for several minutes. Do not pull off a loose claw. Contact a veterinarian if the claw is hanging, split near the base, repeatedly bleeding, very painful, swollen, or producing discharge. Do not give human pain medicine.

Minor Chip or Deeper Tear?

A superficial chip usually affects only the hard keratin tip and causes little discomfort. A deeper tear may expose pink or red tissue, bleed, move when touched, or make the cat limp or lick one toe repeatedly.

Control Minor Bleeding

Use clean gauze or cloth and hold steady pressure. Avoid repeatedly lifting the gauze to check because this can disturb the clot. If bleeding is heavy or will not stop, seek veterinary care.

Do Not Pull a Hanging Claw

A partly attached fragment may still be connected to sensitive tissue. Pulling it can cause severe pain and renewed bleeding. A veterinarian can remove unstable nail material safely and assess whether the nail bed or toe is also injured.

Signs the Injury Needs Veterinary Care

FindingWhy it matters
Split extends toward the baseThe nail bed or quick may be involved
Persistent or recurrent bleedingThe wound may need treatment
Swelling, heat, discharge, or odorPossible infection
Severe limping or toe deformityFracture or deeper injury is possible
Cat will not allow the paw to be touchedPain may be substantial

Keep the Paw Clean

Keep the cat indoors and away from dirty or wet surfaces while the claw is open. Do not soak the paw in harsh disinfectants. Paw bandages can become too tight or trap moisture, so use one only if a veterinary professional has shown you how.

What the Veterinarian May Do

Treatment may include trimming unstable nail material, cleaning the nail bed, controlling bleeding, pain relief, and treatment for infection if present. X-rays may be recommended when the toe itself looks injured.

What Healing Should Look Like

After a minor nail injury, bleeding should stop and the cat should become progressively more willing to use the paw. Persistent licking, renewed bleeding, swelling, heat, discharge, or worsening limping are not signs to simply “give it more time.” Keep the litter box especially clean while the quick is exposed and limit rough climbing until the toe is comfortable.

A damaged claw may look uneven as it grows out. The important question is whether the nail bed remains comfortable and free of infection, not whether the claw looks perfect immediately.

What to Do Next

Control minor bleeding, prevent licking, reduce activity, and never pull a partially attached claw. A tear near the base, exposed quick, persistent bleeding, swelling, or significant pain deserves veterinary care.

faq.question: Can I cut off the loose part of my cat’s claw?
faq.answer: Do not cut a loose fragment if it is painful, bleeding, or still attached near the base. A veterinarian can determine where living tissue begins.

faq.question: Can a torn claw get infected?
faq.answer: Yes. Increasing redness, swelling, heat, discharge, odor, or worsening pain should be checked by a veterinarian.

faq.question: Can I give my cat a human pain reliever?
faq.answer: No. Common human pain medicines can be dangerous or toxic to cats.

title: Broken or Chipped Tooth in Cats: Pain, Infection Risk and Treatment Timing
description: Learn what a chipped or fractured cat tooth can mean, how to recognize pain or pulp exposure, and why veterinary dental treatment may be needed even if the cat still eats.
summary: A chipped or fractured tooth can expose sensitive dentin or the pulp chamber inside the tooth. Cats often hide dental pain, so a broken tooth can look less serious than it feels.
primaryKeyword: broken or chipped tooth in cats
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Cat with a small chipped tooth visible during a gentle veterinary-style mouth check
content:
A chipped or fractured tooth can expose sensitive dentin or the pulp chamber inside the tooth. Cats often hide dental pain, so a broken tooth can look less serious than it feels.

Start With the Pattern, Not a Diagnosis

A tiny superficial chip may not be an emergency, but a fracture with a pink, red, brown, or dark center, bleeding, pain, drooling, food dropping, or facial swelling needs veterinary dental evaluation. Do not test the tooth by pressing or tapping it.

What a Minor Chip Looks Like

A small enamel chip may leave the tooth slightly uneven without exposing deeper tissue. Even then, a veterinary dental examination is useful because the visible crown does not reveal what is happening below the gum line.

When the Pulp Is Exposed

The pulp contains nerves and blood vessels. A fresh pulp exposure may look pink or red, while an older damaged tooth may darken. Exposure can be painful and creates a route for bacteria to enter deeper parts of the tooth.

Signs of Dental Pain

  • Chewing on one side
  • Dropping kibble
  • Approaching food and walking away
  • Drooling or pawing at the mouth
  • Bad breath
  • Refusing hard food

Why Dental X-Rays Matter

Much of a cat’s tooth lies below the gum line. Dental radiographs help evaluate roots, surrounding bone, and other painful dental disease that may not be visible during a quick awake examination.

Treatment Options

Treatment depends on the tooth, depth of fracture, pulp involvement, and overall dental health. Extraction is common for painful non-salvageable teeth, while selected teeth may sometimes be treated with advanced dental procedures.

What to Feed Before the Appointment

If the cat is still eating comfortably, soft food may be easier until the tooth is assessed. Do not force food into the mouth and do not delay care if the cat stops eating.

When It Becomes More Urgent

FindingConcern
Pink/red center or bleedingPulp exposure is possible
Facial swellingInfection may be present
Food refusalPain may be significant
Fracture after major traumaOther jaw or facial injuries may coexist

Why “Still Eating” Does Not Rule Out Dental Pain

Cats often keep eating despite a painful tooth by chewing on the opposite side, swallowing pieces with less chewing, or preferring softer food. That means appetite alone is a poor test of whether a fracture hurts. Watch the mechanics of eating: food dropping, sudden pauses, jaw chattering, one-sided chewing, or walking away after the first bite can be more revealing.

If a tooth has changed color or a fracture exposes deeper tissue, a veterinary dental exam is more useful than waiting for the cat to stop eating.

How to Think About This Sign

A broken tooth can remain painful even when a cat continues to eat. Veterinary dental examination and dental X-rays are the safest way to determine whether the fracture is superficial or has exposed the pulp or damaged the root.

faq.question: Can a cat still eat with a broken tooth?
faq.answer: Yes. Cats often hide oral pain and may continue eating even with a painful fracture.

faq.question: Does every chipped tooth need extraction?
faq.answer: No. Treatment depends on fracture depth, pulp involvement, the tooth involved, and dental X-ray findings.

faq.question: Why did my cat’s broken tooth turn darker?
faq.answer: Color change can indicate damage inside the tooth and should be evaluated by a veterinarian.

title: Swollen Lip in a Cat: Allergy, Dental Disease and Eosinophilic Granuloma
description: Learn why a cat’s lip may swell, how allergy, dental disease, trauma, infection, and eosinophilic granuloma can look similar, and when veterinary care is needed.
summary: A swollen lip in a cat can result from allergy, insect bite, trauma, dental disease, infection, or an inflammatory condition such as eosinophilic granuloma complex. The appearance and recurrence pattern often provide useful clues.
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Cat with a mildly swollen upper lip shown clearly and non-graphically
content:
A swollen lip in a cat can result from allergy, insect bite, trauma, dental disease, infection, or an inflammatory condition such as eosinophilic granuloma complex. The appearance and recurrence pattern often provide useful clues.

What Matters Most Right Now

Arrange veterinary evaluation for a new lip swelling that persists, enlarges, ulcerates, becomes painful, or interferes with eating. Emergency care is appropriate if swelling is rapidly spreading or the cat has breathing difficulty.

Possible Causes

  • Eosinophilic granuloma complex and allergy-related inflammation
  • Dental disease or oral infection
  • Trauma, bites, or insect stings
  • Skin or soft-tissue infection
  • Less common masses or immune-related disease

Eosinophilic Granuloma Complex

Cats can develop characteristic inflammatory lesions on the lips, skin, or inside the mouth. Allergy to fleas, food, or environmental triggers may contribute, although the exact cause can vary from cat to cat.

Look Beyond the Lip

Check whether the cat also has chin lesions, skin itching, mouth ulcers, bad breath, broken teeth, drooling, or difficulty chewing. Recurrent swelling in the same location deserves investigation rather than repeated home treatment.

Red Flags

FindingNext step
Breathing difficulty or rapidly spreading swellingEmergency
Pus, fever, severe painPrompt evaluation
Ulcer that will not healVeterinary examination and possible sampling
Food refusal or heavy droolingPrompt oral examination

What Not to Do

Do not squeeze the lip, apply human creams, or give antihistamines or steroids without veterinary direction. Treatment can hide the pattern and make diagnosis harder.

What the Veterinarian May Do

The examination may include the teeth, gums, tongue, skin, and lymph nodes. Depending on the lesion, the veterinarian may recommend dental imaging, cytology, biopsy, parasite control, or an allergy-focused plan.

Photograph the Swelling Before It Changes

Lip swelling can fluctuate over a day, especially when inflammation or an allergic trigger is involved. A clear photo in natural light can help document whether the lesion is becoming larger, more ulcerated, or more symmetrical. Avoid repeatedly squeezing or rubbing the lip to “test” it; that can increase irritation without identifying the cause.

Recurring lip lesions deserve a broader discussion about dental disease, parasites such as fleas, diet history, and other allergy clues rather than repeated short-term treatment without a diagnosis.

When Observation Should End

A swollen lip is a sign rather than a diagnosis. Persistent, recurrent, ulcerated, painful, or rapidly spreading swelling needs veterinary evaluation so dental, allergic, inflammatory, infectious, and less common causes can be separated.

Read why a cat’s gums may suddenly look bright red. Read why a cat’s whisker pad may swell. Read what sudden facial swelling in cats can mean.

faq.question: Can allergies make a cat’s lip swell?
faq.answer: Yes. Allergy-associated inflammation, including eosinophilic granuloma complex, can affect the lips.

faq.question: Can a bad tooth cause lip or facial swelling?
faq.answer: Yes. Dental infection can cause localized swelling and should be considered when oral pain or bad breath is present.

faq.question: Should I put cream on the swollen lip?
faq.answer: No. Human creams or unprescribed medications can be unsafe and may interfere with diagnosis.

title: Mouth Ulcers in Cats: Why Eating, Drooling and Bad Breath May Suddenly Change
description: Learn why cats can develop painful mouth ulcers, what causes sudden drooling or food refusal, and when oral lesions need prompt veterinary evaluation.
summary: Mouth ulcers can make eating, grooming, and swallowing painful. A cat may drool, develop bad breath, approach food and then back away, or become irritable when the face is touched.
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Cat with a small non-graphic oral ulcer visible during a careful veterinary-style examination
content:
Mouth ulcers can make eating, grooming, and swallowing painful. A cat may drool, develop bad breath, approach food and then back away, or become irritable when the face is touched.

How to Read This Sign

Visible mouth ulcers, heavy drooling, bad breath, or a sudden change in eating deserve veterinary evaluation. Prompt care is especially important if the cat refuses food, seems dehydrated, has widespread oral inflammation, or appears systemically ill.

Why Oral Ulcers Hurt

The mouth contains highly sensitive tissue that is repeatedly exposed to food and saliva. Ulcers can sting with every attempt to eat or groom, which is why cats may reduce intake before owners realize how painful the mouth has become.

Common Causes

  • Severe gingivitis or gingivostomatitis
  • Dental disease and tooth resorption
  • Viral disease such as feline calicivirus
  • Kidney disease and uremic oral injury
  • Trauma, irritants, or foreign material
  • Less common immune-mediated or neoplastic disease

Signs Owners Often Notice

Drooling, bad breath, blood-tinged saliva, food dropping, one-sided chewing, pawing at the mouth, weight loss, and reduced grooming can all accompany oral pain.

Why Food Refusal Matters

Cats that eat very little for too long can develop serious metabolic complications. Mouth pain should therefore not be managed by repeatedly offering more tempting foods for several days without identifying the cause.

What Not to Do

Do not force the mouth open, scrape ulcers, use human mouthwash, or apply pain gels intended for people. Do not force-feed a distressed cat unless a veterinarian specifically instructs you.

What the Veterinarian May Evaluate

A full oral examination may require sedation or anesthesia. Dental X-rays, bloodwork, viral testing, or biopsy may be recommended depending on whether the problem looks dental, inflammatory, systemic, or recurrent.

Why Reduced Eating Changes the Timeline

Mouth pain can turn a cat that appears hungry into a cat that repeatedly approaches food and then backs away. That pattern should be treated as a meaningful appetite problem, not picky eating. Prolonged inadequate intake can create additional health risks in cats, especially those that are overweight.

Until the mouth can be examined, focus on whether the cat is actually consuming food and water rather than whether it shows interest in the bowl.

Where to Go From Here

Mouth ulcers are painful and can quickly affect food intake. Because causes range from dental disease to severe inflammatory or systemic illness, persistent oral lesions and eating changes deserve proper veterinary assessment.

faq.question: Can mouth ulcers make a cat stop eating?
faq.answer: Yes. Oral ulcers can be very painful and may cause a cat to approach food but refuse to chew.

faq.question: Are mouth ulcers always caused by dental disease?
faq.answer: No. Dental inflammation is common, but viral, systemic, traumatic, and other causes are also possible.

faq.question: Can I use human oral pain gel on my cat?
faq.answer: No. Human oral medications may contain ingredients that are unsafe for cats.

title: Cat Abscess After a Fight: How to Spot a Hidden Bite-Wound Infection
description: Learn how small cat bite wounds can seal over and form abscesses, which signs to watch for after a fight, and when swelling, fever, pain, or drainage needs veterinary care.
summary: Cat bite wounds can look tiny on the surface while bacteria are carried deep under the skin. The puncture may seal quickly, trapping infection and allowing an abscess to form over the next several days.
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Cat with a localized swollen area after a fight, shown non-graphically
content:
Cat bite wounds can look tiny on the surface while bacteria are carried deep under the skin. The puncture may seal quickly, trapping infection and allowing an abscess to form over the next several days.

First, Check the Rest of the Cat

If your cat develops a painful lump, fever, lethargy, bad-smelling drainage, or reduced appetite after a fight, contact a veterinarian. Bite wounds near the eye, chest, abdomen, joints, or spine deserve particular attention.

Why Cat Bites Become Infected

Sharp canine teeth can create deep narrow punctures. Because the skin closes faster than the deeper tissue heals, bacteria can multiply in a low-oxygen pocket beneath the surface.

Early Signs

  • Localized heat or swelling
  • Pain when touched
  • Limping
  • Hiding or reduced activity
  • Poor appetite
  • Fever

When an Abscess Opens

A ruptured abscess may release thick, bloody, or foul-smelling material. Drainage can reduce pressure, but an open abscess still needs assessment because infected tissue or deeper pockets may remain.

What Not to Do

Do not squeeze the lump aggressively, insert objects into a wound, or start leftover antibiotics. Antibiotic choice and duration depend on the wound, and some abscesses require drainage or flushing.

When the Wound Is More Urgent

FindingConcern
Swelling near the eyeEye and facial structures are at risk
Difficulty breathing after chest biteEmergency
Severe limping or swelling over a jointDeeper infection possible
Weakness, fever, food refusalSystemic illness possible

What the Veterinarian May Do

Treatment may include clipping fur, opening and flushing the abscess, pain relief, and antibiotics when appropriate. The veterinarian may also discuss vaccination and FIV/FeLV risk depending on the fight history.

The Skin Wound May Be Smaller Than the Infection

A bite puncture can close over quickly, so the visible mark may underestimate what is happening beneath the skin. A cat that becomes quiet, warm, sore, or unwilling to eat a few days after a fight may have developed a pocket of infection even when you cannot find an obvious open wound.

Your veterinarian may also discuss testing for feline retroviruses depending on the cat’s vaccination status, outdoor exposure, and bite history. That decision is based on individual risk rather than the presence of an abscess alone.

The Practical Takeaway

A fight wound can become infected even when the original puncture is hard to find. New swelling, pain, fever, drainage, or appetite loss after a fight should be treated as a possible abscess and examined promptly.

Related Virixoo Guides

Read how to approach a new lump under a cat’s skin. Read why a cat’s sore may fail to heal. Read what sudden facial swelling can mean.

faq.question: How long after a fight can an abscess appear?
faq.answer: Swelling may not be obvious immediately. It can develop over the following days as infection builds beneath the skin.

faq.question: If the abscess bursts, is the problem solved?
faq.answer: No. Drainage may reduce pressure, but the wound still needs assessment for deeper infection and appropriate treatment.

faq.question: Can cat fights spread FIV or FeLV?
faq.answer: Bite exposure is relevant to infectious-disease risk, especially for FIV, so discuss the circumstances with your veterinarian.

title: Black Tarry Stool in Cats: Why Melena Can Signal Internal Bleeding
description: Learn why black, sticky, tar-like stool in cats can indicate digested blood and when melena, weakness, vomiting, or pale gums needs urgent veterinary attention.
summary: Black, shiny, sticky, tar-like stool can represent melena, which is digested blood that has passed through the gastrointestinal tract. True melena is different from ordinary dark-brown stool.
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Cat owner noticing unusually black tar-like stool in a litter box, shown cleanly and non-graphically
content:
Black, shiny, sticky, tar-like stool can represent melena, which is digested blood that has passed through the gastrointestinal tract. True melena is different from ordinary dark-brown stool.

The Safest Next Step

If your cat’s stool is genuinely black, tarry, sticky, and unusually foul-smelling, contact a veterinarian promptly. Urgent care is especially important when black stool occurs with pale gums, weakness, vomiting, collapse, rapid breathing, or reduced appetite.

Why Blood Can Turn Black

Blood originating higher in the digestive tract can be digested before it leaves the body, turning the stool black rather than bright red. This is why melena can be a sign of internal gastrointestinal bleeding.

Possible Causes

  • Stomach or intestinal ulceration
  • Severe gastrointestinal inflammation
  • Foreign material or trauma
  • Clotting disorders or toxin exposure
  • Swallowed blood from the mouth or nose
  • Certain medications that irritate the gastrointestinal tract

Dark Brown vs. Tarry Black

Normal stool can vary in shade. Melena is typically not just dark; it is often jet-black, sticky, shiny, and difficult to wipe away. Take a clear photo and, if practical, bring a fresh sample to the veterinary clinic.

Signs of Blood Loss

FindingWhy it matters
Pale or white gumsAnemia or significant blood loss is possible
Weakness or collapseEmergency concern
Rapid breathingMay accompany anemia or shock
Vomiting blood or coffee-ground materialActive upper GI bleeding possible

Medication History Matters

Tell the veterinarian about every medication and supplement the cat has received. Never give human anti-inflammatory medicines unless a veterinarian specifically prescribes them for that cat.

What the Veterinarian May Check

Evaluation may include gum color and circulation, blood tests to check red blood cells and clotting, abdominal imaging, and investigation for gastrointestinal disease, toxins, or bleeding elsewhere.

Medication and Exposure History Matters

Tell the veterinarian about every medication, supplement, toxin exposure, and recent procedure—not only products labeled for cats. Gastrointestinal bleeding can be influenced by clotting problems, severe disease, or medication effects, and the timeline may change which tests are most useful.

Do not give human pain relievers to a cat with black stool. Some common human medications are dangerous to cats and may complicate bleeding or kidney injury.

The Safest Takeaway

True black tarry stool should be treated as possible digested blood, not simply a stool-color variation. The combination of melena with pale gums, weakness, or collapse is especially urgent.

faq.question: Is every dark stool melena?
faq.answer: No. Melena is typically black, sticky, shiny, and tar-like rather than simply dark brown.

faq.question: Can swallowed blood make stool black?
faq.answer: Yes. Blood swallowed from the mouth or nose can sometimes darken stool, but the source still needs investigation.

faq.question: Why are pale gums with black stool more urgent?
faq.answer: That combination may indicate clinically important blood loss and anemia.

title: Bloated Belly in a Cat: Gas, Fluid, Organ Enlargement or Emergency?
description: Learn what can make a cat’s abdomen look enlarged and how to recognize when rapid distension, pain, breathing changes, or weakness needs urgent veterinary care.
summary: A cat’s abdomen can look enlarged because of weight gain, gas, constipation, fluid accumulation, pregnancy, organ enlargement, a mass, or other disease.
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Cat with a visibly enlarged abdomen while resting indoors
content:
A cat’s abdomen can look enlarged because of weight gain, gas, constipation, fluid accumulation, pregnancy, organ enlargement, a mass, or other disease. The speed of change and the cat’s overall comfort are more informative than shape alone.

The First Decision to Make

A gradually round abdomen in an otherwise comfortable cat is different from a suddenly distended, painful belly. Seek prompt care if the abdomen enlarges rapidly or occurs with breathing difficulty, repeated vomiting, weakness, inability to urinate, severe pain, or collapse.

Common Reasons the Abdomen Looks Larger

  • Weight gain
  • Constipation or gastrointestinal distension
  • Fluid in the abdomen
  • Organ enlargement or a mass
  • Pregnancy or uterine disease in intact females
  • Parasites, especially in kittens

Why Speed Matters

A change developing over hours is more concerning than a stable shape that has changed slowly over months. Rapid abdominal distension can accompany serious gastrointestinal, urinary, reproductive, circulatory, or bleeding problems.

Weight Gain vs. Distension

Simple weight gain usually changes the body more broadly. A cat that is losing weight over the spine or hips while the abdomen becomes larger may have fluid, organ enlargement, pregnancy, or another underlying condition.

Red Flags

FindingConcern
Hard, painful, rapidly enlarging abdomenUrgent assessment
Repeated straining with little or no urinePossible urinary obstruction
Breathing difficultyEmergency
Weakness, pale gums, collapseInternal bleeding or shock possible
Repeated vomitingGI obstruction or severe illness possible

What Not to Do

Do not press repeatedly on a painful abdomen, give human gas remedies, or assume litter-box straining means constipation until you confirm urine is being produced.

What the Veterinarian May Do

The veterinarian may palpate the abdomen and bladder and recommend bloodwork, X-rays, ultrasound, fecal testing, or sampling of abdominal fluid depending on the pattern.

Do Not Try to Diagnose the Swelling by Pressing on It

Fluid, enlarged organs, fat, intestinal contents, pregnancy, and masses can all change the abdominal outline, and they cannot be reliably separated by squeezing the belly at home. Repeated palpation can also be painful in a cat with abdominal disease.

A veterinarian may use physical examination together with ultrasound, radiographs, bloodwork, or fluid sampling when needed. The speed of enlargement and the cat’s breathing, appetite, urination, and comfort help determine how urgently those tests are needed.

The Safer Takeaway

A larger abdomen can be harmless weight gain or a sign of important disease. Rapid change, pain, breathing problems, urinary difficulty, vomiting, weakness, or weight loss elsewhere in the body makes veterinary assessment more urgent.

faq.question: Can constipation make a cat’s belly look bloated?
faq.answer: Yes, but abdominal enlargement has many possible causes, so persistent or painful distension should be examined.

faq.question: Is a bloated belly an emergency?
faq.answer: It can be when it develops rapidly or occurs with pain, breathing difficulty, repeated vomiting, collapse, or inability to urinate.

faq.question: Can a cat be losing weight but still have a large belly?
faq.answer: Yes. Fluid accumulation, organ enlargement, pregnancy, or other disease can enlarge the abdomen while the rest of the body becomes thinner.

title: Nosebleeds in Cats: Trauma, High Blood Pressure and Other Causes to Check
description: Learn what can cause a cat nosebleed, how trauma, infection, clotting disorders, high blood pressure, or nasal disease change the concern, and when veterinary care is urgent.
summary: Nosebleeds are uncommon enough in cats that a new episode deserves attention. Causes range from trauma and nasal irritation to high blood pressure, dental disease, clotting problems, toxins, infection, or a nasal mass.
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Cat with a small non-graphic amount of blood at one nostril while resting calmly
content:
Nosebleeds are uncommon enough in cats that a new episode deserves attention. Causes range from trauma and nasal irritation to high blood pressure, dental disease, clotting problems, toxins, infection, or a nasal mass.

What Owners Should Notice First

Keep the cat calm, discourage rubbing at the nose, and contact a veterinarian if bleeding is heavy, recurrent, lasts more than a few minutes, or is accompanied by weakness, breathing difficulty, facial swelling, or pale gums.

One Nostril or Both?

Bleeding from one nostril may point toward a localized nasal problem, trauma, dental disease, or a mass. Bleeding from both nostrils can also occur with local disease but may increase concern about clotting or systemic causes.

Possible Causes

  • Trauma or a foreign object
  • High blood pressure
  • Dental disease extending toward the nasal cavity
  • Clotting disorders or anticoagulant toxins
  • Infection or severe inflammation
  • Nasal tumors or polyps

What to Do During a Small Nosebleed

Keep the cat quiet and cool. Avoid manipulating the nose. If tolerated, a cool compress over the bridge of the nose may help, but do not obstruct breathing or force handling.

What Not to Do

Do not insert cotton swabs, tissue, or packing material into the nostril. Do not tip the cat’s head backward and do not give aspirin or other human medication.

Red Flags

FindingConcern
Heavy or persistent bleedingUrgent evaluation
Pale gums or weaknessBlood loss or systemic disease
Difficulty breathingEmergency
Facial swelling or repeated one-sided dischargeLocal disease needs investigation
Possible rodenticide exposureEmergency toxicology concern

Why Blood Pressure Matters

Older cats with kidney disease or hyperthyroidism can develop hypertension. High blood pressure can damage fragile blood vessels and may also cause eye problems or sudden vision loss.

What the Veterinarian May Check

Evaluation may include blood pressure, blood count, clotting tests, oral and dental examination, and nasal imaging depending on whether the bleeding is recurrent or one-sided.

What Not to Put in the Nose

Do not pack the nostril with tissue, cotton swabs, powders, or medication. Do not tilt the cat’s head sharply backward or repeatedly wipe inside the nostril, because agitation can prolong bleeding and objects placed in the nose can cause additional injury.

If the episode stops, note which nostril bled, how long it lasted, whether sneezing preceded it, and whether the cat has had bruising, weakness, dental problems, or recent trauma. Recurrent episodes are more useful diagnostically when this history is recorded.

What to Do Next

A single tiny nosebleed after obvious minor trauma may settle, but unexplained, recurrent, or significant bleeding needs veterinary assessment to identify local and systemic causes.

faq.question: Can high blood pressure cause nosebleeds in cats?
faq.answer: It can contribute to bleeding and is especially important to consider in older cats or cats with kidney or thyroid disease.

faq.question: Should I put tissue inside my cat’s nostril?
faq.answer: No. Packing the nostril at home can worsen distress or interfere with breathing.

faq.question: What if the bleeding stops quickly?
faq.answer: A one-time minor episode may settle, but unexplained or recurrent nosebleeds still deserve veterinary discussion.

title: Yellow Gums or Eyes in Cats: What Jaundice Can Mean
description: Learn why yellow gums, skin, or whites of the eyes in cats can signal jaundice and how liver disease, red blood cell destruction, or bile-flow problems are investigated.
summary: Yellow discoloration of the gums, whites of the eyes, inner ears, or skin is called jaundice or icterus . It occurs when bilirubin accumulates in the body and is a sign of disease rather than a diagnosis by itself.
primaryKeyword: yellow gums or eyes in cats
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Cat with subtle yellow discoloration of the gums and eye whites shown non-graphically
content:
Yellow discoloration of the gums, whites of the eyes, inner ears, or skin is called jaundice or icterus. It occurs when bilirubin accumulates in the body and is a sign of disease rather than a diagnosis by itself.

The First Decision Is Urgency

A cat with newly yellow gums, eyes, or skin should be evaluated promptly. Jaundice can result from red blood cell destruction, liver disease, or blockage of bile flow. Food refusal, vomiting, weakness, dark urine, or rapid worsening increases urgency.

Where Yellowing Is Easiest to See

Look at lightly pigmented gums, the whites of the eyes, and the inner ear pinnae in good light. Mild jaundice can be subtle, so comparison with the cat’s normal color can help.

Three Broad Categories of Causes

Before the Liver

Rapid destruction of red blood cells can generate more bilirubin than the liver can process.

Within the Liver

Liver inflammation, hepatic lipidosis, toxins, infection, and other liver disorders can interfere with bilirubin handling.

After the Liver

Obstruction or inflammation affecting bile flow can prevent bilirubin from leaving the body normally.

Why Appetite Matters So Much

Cats that stop eating can develop hepatic lipidosis, particularly when overweight. Jaundice combined with several days of poor intake is therefore especially important to address quickly.

Other Signs to Watch For

  • Dark yellow, orange, or brown urine
  • Vomiting or diarrhea
  • Weight loss
  • Weakness or hiding
  • Abdominal discomfort
  • Pale gums in addition to yellowing

What Not to Do

Do not try to treat jaundice with supplements or force-feed a nauseated or weak cat without veterinary advice. The underlying cause must be identified.

What the Veterinarian May Check

Evaluation often includes bloodwork, urine testing, and abdominal imaging. Additional tests may be needed to distinguish red-cell destruction from primary liver disease or bile-flow obstruction.

Jaundice Is a Sign, Not a Liver Diagnosis

Yellow tissue tells you that bilirubin has accumulated, but it does not tell you where the problem started. Red-blood-cell destruction, liver dysfunction, and impaired bile flow can look similar from the outside and require different treatment.

If the cat is also eating poorly, tell the veterinarian how long intake has been reduced. Cats—particularly overweight cats—can develop serious liver complications when they do not eat enough, so appetite history is an important part of the workup.

Do Not Wait for Worse Signs

Jaundice in cats is a significant finding. Because it can reflect blood disease, liver disease, or bile obstruction, new yellow gums or eyes should prompt veterinary evaluation rather than home monitoring.

faq.question: Is jaundice in cats an emergency?
faq.answer: It is always important and should be evaluated promptly. The urgency is higher when the cat is weak, not eating, vomiting, or rapidly worsening.

faq.question: Can not eating cause jaundice in cats?
faq.answer: Prolonged poor intake can contribute to hepatic lipidosis, a serious liver disorder that can cause jaundice.

faq.question: Can yellow eyes come from anemia?
faq.answer: Some conditions that destroy red blood cells can cause both anemia and bilirubin accumulation, so blood tests are often important.

title: Cat Suddenly Collapses or Faints: Emergency Causes Owners Should Know
description: Learn what sudden collapse or fainting can mean in cats, how heart, circulation, breathing, neurologic, metabolic, or bleeding emergencies are considered, and what to do immediately.
summary: A cat that suddenly collapses or appears to faint should be treated as an emergency sign until proven otherwise.
author: Virixoo Editorial Team
alt: Cat lying on its side after a sudden collapse while the owner prepares for emergency veterinary care
content:
A cat that suddenly collapses or appears to faint should be treated as an emergency sign until proven otherwise. Collapse can result from heart disease, abnormal heart rhythm, severe anemia, internal bleeding, low blood sugar, breathing problems, neurologic disease, or other systemic emergencies.

When Waiting Is the Wrong Choice

If your cat collapses, becomes unresponsive, cannot stand, has blue or very pale gums, or struggles to breathe, seek emergency veterinary care. Even if the cat seems normal again within minutes, the underlying cause can still be serious.

Fainting vs. Seizure

Fainting often involves sudden loss of posture with relatively quick recovery. Seizures may include paddling, jaw movements, drooling, urination, or a period of confusion afterward. In real life the two can overlap, so a video—if safely obtained—can help the veterinarian.

Important Causes

  • Heart disease or arrhythmia
  • Internal bleeding or severe anemia
  • Breathing or oxygen problems
  • Low blood sugar or metabolic disturbance
  • Neurologic disease or seizure
  • Toxin exposure or medication error

What to Do Immediately

Place the cat on a flat surface, keep the airway unobstructed, minimize handling, and prepare for transport. Note gum color and breathing if you can do so without delaying care.

Do Not Give Food or Water

Do not force food, water, or medication into the mouth of a weak or poorly responsive cat because aspiration is possible.

Emergency Red Flags

FindingMeaning
Open-mouth breathing or blue gumsEmergency oxygen problem
Very pale gumsSevere anemia or circulation failure possible
Repeated collapseSerious underlying disease likely
Seizure lasting several minutes or repeated seizuresEmergency neurologic concern
Recent toxin or human medication exposureEmergency toxicology concern

If the Cat Seems Normal Again

Do not assume the problem has resolved. Intermittent heart rhythm problems, fainting, seizures, and internal disease can leave a cat looking normal between episodes.

What the Veterinarian May Evaluate

Testing may include blood pressure, bloodwork, glucose measurement, ECG, heart imaging, chest or abdominal imaging, or neurologic evaluation depending on the episode.

A Brief Recovery Does Not Make Collapse Benign

Some cats stand up and appear nearly normal soon after a fainting episode or brief collapse. That recovery is useful information, but it does not rule out heart rhythm problems, internal bleeding, low blood sugar, or other serious causes. Record how long the episode lasted and what the cat was doing immediately beforehand.

For transport, keep the cat quiet in a carrier or on a flat supportive surface, minimize handling, and call the emergency clinic while you are on the way if possible. Do not offer food, water, or medication to a cat that is not fully alert.

Why Prompt Care Matters

Sudden collapse is an emergency symptom, not a diagnosis. Stabilization and evaluation are more important than trying to determine the exact cause at home.

faq.question: What if my cat fainted but is acting normal now?
faq.answer: The cat still needs veterinary assessment because intermittent heart, circulation, metabolic, or neurologic problems can leave a cat looking normal between episodes.

faq.question: How can I tell fainting from a seizure?
faq.answer: It can be difficult. Seizures more often include paddling, drooling, jaw movements, or a confused recovery period, but overlap is possible.

faq.question: Should I give sugar or food after a collapse?
faq.answer: Do not put food, water, or medication into the mouth of a weak or poorly responsive cat unless a veterinarian specifically instructs you.
